<meta>continues from previous page: ...as if</meta> with the best honey, and by stirring the mass, you will soften it. The whole must be divided, as if into very large olives; one of these should be consumed around the second hour <note>about 8:00 AM</note>, and another around the tenth hour <note>about 4:00 PM</note>, and they will suffer no harm from hunger. There is another composition of the same kind, taking a <term>semisextarius</term> <gloss>about half a pint</gloss> of Attic sesame, and a half-part of honey, a <term>cotyle</term> <gloss>about half a pint</gloss> of oil, and a <term>choenix</term> <gloss>about a quart</gloss> of cleaned sweet almonds. One must grind and sift the sesame and almonds after drying them; then, peeling the squills <note>sea onions</note> all around, cutting off the roots and leaves, and slicing them into small pieces, it is necessary to place them in a mortar and pound them until they are perfectly smooth. Soon after, knead a part of honey equal to the pounded squills uniformly together with the oil, and by pouring it into a pot and placing it over coals, it must be stirred here and there with a wooden spatula until everything is mixed. When the mass has become solid, it will be worthwhile to divide it into small morsels; anyone taking one in the morning and another in the evening will have sufficient nourishment. This medicine is indeed beneficial for an army; for being sweet, it brings satiety and takes away thirst. We have excerpted these things from a certain manuscript scholium <note>an ancient marginal note or commentary</note> on the book of Heron <note>Heron of Alexandria</note> in the Vatican library. We have seen the same composition in Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a Byzantine scholar</note>, in the fifth book of military affairs, where he describes other similar things of this sort.

->*From which fruits wines may be made.*<-

### CHAPTER XXI.

Now we shall review the fruits from which wines may be made; first those commonly made by our ancestors, but with a twofold distinction. For some are for remedies, of which the books of Physicians are full, and others are for general use. The types are various and almost infinite, according to the differences of places and nations; for what is given to one is denied to another. First,

->*Wine from palms*<-

Pliny said that in the East, wine is made from these, and he lists fifty kinds of palms and the differences of the wines made from them. Among these, the <term>caryotae</term> <gloss>nut-dates</gloss> are most celebrated, being very rich in juice, from which the principal wines of the East are made. They are harmful to the head, from which the fruit takes its name <note>derived from the Greek *karos*, meaning a heavy sleep or stupor</note>. <summary>Della Porta provides a recipe for a nutritious military ration based on squill and honey and begins a catalog of fruit wines, starting with date palm wine from the Middle East.</summary>
